newsitem.title: USA: Investment demand still key to silver price - CPM.
newsitem.headline: Investment demand still key to silver price - CPM.

text.p: Investment demand is the pivotal factor in the direction of silver prices, though the underlying fundamentals for silver are continuing to improve, as demand exceeds supply and above-ground inventories are drawn down, New York based industry consultants, CPM Group said Tuesday.

"Investors are monitoring the silver market closely, with the view that the huge shortfalls in newly refined silver supply relative to fabrication demand will eventually lead to a period of significantly higher prices," CPM Group said in its 1997 silver survey published Tuesday.

"That said it is unlikely that investors will re-enter the silver market forcefully without a sharp correction in the US and other equities markets, or some other major economic or financial disturbance," the survey said.

"Should EMU (European Monetary Union due in 1999) stumble, some investors would likely seek shelter in silver, gold and platinum against erratic movements in the currency markets and related European financial assets."
Investors are expected to remain net sellers of silver this year, selling some 188.3 million ounces of silver bullion on a net basis, the survey said.
COMEX nearby active March silver futures were down 2.5 cents at $5.175 an ounce midmorning Tuesday, after trading in a $5.27-4.66 range in 1996.
But "silver prices reasonably could rise as high as $6.00 by late 1997", as demand exceeds supply, drawing down above ground inventories to 46 year lows, the report said.

"Already some fabricators are beginning to take steps to protect themselves as inventories could fall to only about 4.7 months worth of demand," CPM managing director Jeffrey Christian told analysts at a briefing.
The absence of investors in silver last year led to an easing in price volatility, although silver remained the most volatile of the preciouse metals, the report said.
The difference between the low and high COMEX settlement price in 1996 was $1.12, the lowest since 1992.
Measured on a monthly basis, volatility for the year peaked at 8.1 pct in June and hit a low of 3.9 pct in December.
Volatility is here defined as the spread between the monthly high and low prices, as a percentage of the low price for the month.
Futures trading activity in silver declined for the second consecutive year in 1996, the report noted.
Trading volume on the New York, Tokyo and Chicago exchanges fell to 25.1 billion ounces in 1996, down 8.0 pct from 1995.
Total open interest at year-end 1996 stood at 521.2 million ounces, down 4.8 pct from 1995.
"This was the lowest annual trading volume and year-end open interest since 1993 and 1992 respectively," the report said.
COMEX remained by far the largest silver futures market by volume, accounting for 96.9 pct of total trade.
COMEX market share increased in 1996, as the volume and open interest dropped more sharply on TOCOM and the CBOT than in New York.
Total open interest in COMEX silver options slipped 12.7 pct in 1996 to 296.6 million ounces.
But open interest in calls rose 2.5 pct to 246.5 million ounces, while put option open interest fell sharply to 50.1 million ounces.

"It is interesting to note that the put/call ratio at the end of 1996 was at an unusually low level - a level only seen once before in the COMEX silver option market, and that was at the cyclical bottom in silver prices in early 1993," the report said.
In the bullion market, the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) released data on bullion market trading for the first time in January 1997.

The data showed around 248 million ounces of silver trades, including spot transactions, forwards, options and other silver trades, were cleared through the eight London silver clearing banks per day in December 1996.
